newsitem.title: GERMANY: German public TV launches "Phoenix" info channel.
newsitem.headline: German public TV launches "Phoenix" info channel.

text.p: Germany's public TV networks launched the Phoenix information channel on Monday, kicking off a new style of commentary-free news broadcasting.

Phoenix blends CNN-style coverage of breaking news with live broadcasts of events such as parliamentary debates in Germany and other European capitals modelled after the C-SPAN channel in the United States.

In contrast with the fast-paced 24-hour news delivery of CNN or its German counterpart N-TV, Phoenix aims to put journalists in the back seat, presenting events in full and letting viewers form their own opinions.
"This is a different form of presenting information," Fritz Pleitgen, head of broadcaster Westdeutsche Rundfunk (WDR) and father of the new channel, told Reuters.

Standing before a wall of flickering TV screens in the hectic Phoenix control room, Pleitgen said the new channel, which will broadcast its programmes for 16 hours a day, should not be compared with conventional news broadcasters.
"It is not a news channel, it is an information programme. We want to present events to viewers in such a way that allows them to make up their own minds about things," he said.
Phoenix will enjoy a luxury ordinary news broadcasts do not have. Without the usual time constraints, it will show parliamentary debates, scientific conferences and other events at full length.

"We will not bring news updates every 15 minutes -- what I would call information fast food. We are not counting on effects and opinion, but rather information," said Klaus Radke, one of Phoenix's two managing directors.

A project of Germany's main public broadcasting networks -- ARD and ZDF -- Phoenix has 68 journalists and production employees. The costs of producing Phoenix have not been revealed but it will be financed through the fees viewers pay for public television and will carry no advertising.
The channel's first live broadcast in its programme slot called "Phoenix on the Scene" showed German President Roman Herzog as he accepted an honorary doctorate at a Tokyo university.

Other broadcasts this week include a documentary on Bill Gates, founder of software giant Microsoft Corp, two sessions of the German Constitutional Court, coverage of the British election campaign and a trade union conference in Berlin.

The channel is also finalising a cooperation deal with C-SPAN to air the U.S. channel's three hour programme on Europe and a joint call-in programme allowing German and American viewers to call in and comment on programmes, said Radke.

Like C-SPAN, Phoenix will also air historical documentaries and reenactments. The first of these will be a recreation of the 1942 Wannsee Conference, where the Nazi elite decided to annihilate European Jewry.
These programmes are not the kind that win big prime-time audiences, but that is not the intention.
"Our primary goal is not to win in the ratings, but rather to create a brand name in information broadcasting," said Barbara Groth, Phoenix's second managing director.
So far Phoenix can only be seen by around six million German households over the European Astra satellite network and in cable TV networks in just a handful of German cities.
But it has not yet gained access to the national cable TV network, which has some 16 million subscribers.
The channel expects to be available to more than 80 percent of German viewers by the end of the year, but in order for that to happen other channels could be thrown off the cable network.
There are 30 channels in the analogue cable network. But there are so many broadcasters that some channels have to share a slot and sometimes are forced out to make room for others.

Authorities in North Rhine-Westphalia state, for example, are widely expected to dump commercial channel Kabel 1 for Phoenix, while Bavarian media regulators have said other public broadcasting channels must leave to make room for Phoenix.
But the squeeze for cable space should ease when German telecoms giant Deutsche Telekom later this year finally opens 150 digital channels.
